Roughly, I would paraphrase this genre as: Action adventures with Minecraft tech. Hear me out, this is not the "Bacon and ice cream and popcorn in a blender should make for the most marvelous shake!" approach.

Imagine a Deus Ex game (There are currently four, you should invest time in at least the original, in Invisible War, and in Human Revolution.) where you can't just carry around and hence repurpose the auto-turrets like in HR, but also all other relevant objects (hackable components that control something, cameras, etc.; repurposing those obviously is more complex). But not only that: With enough realistic effort you can even break walls (almost never; don't think wall-break augmentation, ok), the pipes are not just decoration, and if you break the machine at the end of Deus Ex 1 of which you have to push a few buttons to win, you'd have to repair it first. With what parts? Here, you can rather just think "Minecraft".

Minecraft mob grinders, that's the angle I'm coming from. I have to describe those a bit, skip to "XXX" if you know them already. In Minecraft, monsters only spawn at night, but they actually just require darkness. They can, just like you, fall to their death, get killed by lava or cacti, etc., and they even drop something (quasi) useful when they die. Just like you, they are moved by flowing water and can also drown in water. You can alter the Minecraft world in kind of any way you like. Someone saw all this and realized: "WTF!" And they built a place that was completely encased, so that it was dark. They also added flowing water, so that spawning monsters would be dragged to a desired place. That desired place happened to be a hole with a long drop. XXX The awesome thing is that, guess what happened: Exactly what intuition would tell you. You stand down there, monsters rain down and turn into useful stuff. That's just one very cheap type of mob trap. How do the more elaborate ones work? You can think that up yourself! And what to do with the drops? Well, did I mention that those are dragged by flowing water, too?

You see, the simple world elements and simple world simulation allow for awesome emergent gameplay and effects. I heard from time to time that Mojang wasn't too happy with the mob trap concept, probably because it could cause lag on servers and would imbalance the game. In any case: What if we would devise a game whose world consists of parts, like Minecraft, and whose elements and world simulation are specifically designed not just to give you a reasonably believable reality, but which also intently allow for a lot of emergent gameplay/constructs?

And then we mix it with a game kind of like Deus Ex, where you have your lone ranger self-experience with missions and tools, and where you could hack a system not just via some cheap minigame but e.g. by finding the right wires or pipes in the right wall and manipulating them in your interest? Or you build something new which has interesting emergent behavior like mob traps (only it wouldn't actually be the specific example of mob traps)?

A world where you know that you're not just staring at a beautiful 3D painting, instead everything that happens does so as emergent behavior resulting from simple parts. Where "noclip" wouldn't show you that everything is just a facade, because it wouldn't be. Where new secondary mission objectives pop up because an intently placed firefight in which you weren't as successful as you could have been, or the random generator wasn't friendly, pipes or wires had been damaged, making the main exit door to the next part of Doom 3's station on Mars unreachable. You need to repair that before moving on.
